question: What do implementers and measurements report about Head-of-Line (HOL) blocking in HTTP/2 versus HTTP/3: the measured effect of packet loss (with numbers, loss rates and setups), how implementations handle QPACK blocking in practice, how HTTP/2 deployments work around TCP HOL blocking, and how prioritization interacts with HOL blocking?

sources.rank_basis: tier B: class (company engineering blog: Fastly’s own blog; the page credits the author as Patrick McManus, Distinguished Engineer, Fastly, line 331)
tier B: project's own home (H2O server's official configuration docs), for facts about H2O
tier B: project's own home (cloudflare/quiche repository, source at release tag 0.22.0), for facts about quiche

facts.summary: Typical packet loss rates given: about 0.01% on high-speed cabled networks and rarely above 2% even on the worst cellular networks; loss and jitter are often bursty.
facts.quote: Especially on high-speed, cabled networks, packet loss rates are on the order of 0.01%. Even on the worst cellular networks, you will rarely see rates higher than 2% in practice. This is combined with the fact that packet loss and also jitter (delay variations in the network), are often bursty.

facts.summary: Worked example of TCP HOL blocking: when TCP packet 2 is lost, packet 3 waits in the receive buffer for the retransmission, which takes at least one round trip, even though part of it belongs to another HTTP/2 stream.
facts.quote: TCP keeps packet 3 in its receive buffer until it receives the retransmitted copy of packet 2 (which takes at least 1 round-trip to the server), after which it can pass both to the browser in the correct order. Put differently: the lost packet 2 is HOL blocking packet 3!

facts.summary: As deployed, HTTP/2 is reported as typically as fast as or slightly faster than HTTP/1.1 in most conditions.
facts.quote: HTTP/2 as it is currently deployed in browsers and servers is typically as fast or slightly faster than HTTP/1.1 in most conditions

facts.summary: Browsers often still open several parallel HTTP/2 connections, because sites shard resources across servers or because of security-related side effects.
facts.quote: browsers often still open multiple parallel HTTP/2 connections (either because sites still shard their resources over different servers, or because of security-related side-effects), thus getting the best of both worlds

facts.summary: On slower networks with higher packet loss, HTTP/1.1 over 6 connections can still beat HTTP/2 over one connection, often because of TCP-level HOL blocking.
facts.quote: there are also some cases (especially on slower networks with higher packet loss) where HTTP/1.1 on 6 connections will still outshine HTTP/2 on one connection, which is often due to the TCP-level HOL blocking problem

facts.summary: QPACK is described as letting the implementation choose its own trade-off between possible HOL blocking and compression ratio.
facts.quote: QPACK is HTTP/3’s version of HPACK and allows a self-chosen trade-off between potential HOL blocking and compression performance

loc.heading: HOL blocking in HTTP/3 over QUIC

facts.summary: QUIC keeps byte order within one stream, so its HOL blocking removal only helps when several streams are active; a lone stream hit by loss is still HOL blocked.
facts.quote: QUIC’s HOL blocking removal only works if there are multiple resource streams active at the same time. … However, if there is only a single stream active at a given moment, any loss will impact that lonely stream and we will still be HOL blocked, even in QUIC.

loc.heading: Do QUIC and HTTP/3 really completely remove HOL blocking?

facts.summary: The page sets two conflicting scheduling goals: multiplexing streams (12121212) to benefit from QUIC's HOL blocking removal, against sending sequentially (11112222) so browsers can process core resources sooner.
facts.quote: To profit from QUIC’s HOL blocking removal: send resources multiplexed (12121212) … To make sure browsers can process core resources ASAP: send resources sequentially (11112222)

loc.heading: Do QUIC and HTTP/3 really completely remove HOL blocking?

facts.summary: Worked example with one burst of 8 lost packets across 2 streams: with sequential sending HOL removal barely helps; it helps only if the loss happens to hit one stream; if the loss spans both streams, both are HOL blocked.
facts.quote: we assume we have a single burst of 8 lost packets while we are downloading 2 streams (green and purple) … Here, we see that QUIC’s HOL blocking removal indeed doesn’t really help all that much … The 8 lost packets are distributed across the two streams. This means that both streams are now HOL blocked

loc.heading: Do QUIC and HTTP/3 really completely remove HOL blocking?

facts.summary: Most QUIC implementations rarely put data from more than one stream in the same packet, since losing such a packet HOL blocks every stream in it.
facts.quote: most QUIC implementations very rarely create packets containing data from more than 1 stream at the same time. If one of those packets is lost, it immediately leads to HOL blocking for all streams in the single packet!

loc.heading: Do QUIC and HTTP/3 really completely remove HOL blocking?

facts.summary: In December 2020 the author had no final measurements; early experiments led him to expect that QUIC's HOL blocking removal helps little for web performance, with a large effect only on networks with much packet loss.
facts.quote: I don’t have final measurements to go on. However, my personal gut feeling (which -is- backed by my results from several early experiments) says that QUIC’s HOL blocking removal probably won’t actually help all that much for Web performance … We saw that it would probably only have a large impact on networks with a lot of packet loss.

loc.heading: Do QUIC and HTTP/3 really completely remove HOL blocking?

facts.summary: QUIC's congestion control runs per connection, not per stream, so loss on any stream slows down all streams of the HTTP/3 connection.
facts.quote: QUIC’s congestion control is still done at the connection level, and not per-stream. This means that even though the streams are conceptually independent, they all still impact QUIC’s singular, per-connection congestion controller, causing slowdowns if there is loss on any of the stream.

facts.summary: A 2016 Fastly-side evaluation showed page load times improving by 29% on mobile and 5% on desktop after moving to HTTP/2.
facts.quote: It showed page load times at his organization to have improved by 29% on mobile and a more modest 5% on desktop when transitioned to HTTP/2.

loc.heading: The connections that HTTP/2 left behind

facts.summary: A 2016 Fastly study found HTTP/2 fares worse against HTTP/1 the higher the packet loss, because all exchanges share one TCP connection with in-order delivery.
facts.quote: Hooman illustrates that the higher the packet loss the worse HTTP/2 performs in comparison to HTTP/1. This is mostly because of HTTP/2’s use of just one TCP connection for all exchanges compared to HTTP/1’s use of one connection per concurrent exchange and the interaction of packet loss with TCP’s congestion control and in-order delivery guarantee.

loc.heading: The connections that HTTP/2 left behind

facts.summary: Rule-of-thumb loss thresholds from that study: below 0.5% loss HTTP/2 helped, between 0.5% and 1.5% gains and losses roughly cancelled, above 1.5% HTTP/2 hurt.
facts.quote: as a rough rule of thumb, connections with less than 0.5% packet loss benefited from HTTP/2, those with between 0.5% and 1.5% loss benefited roughly as much as they sacrificed by using HTTP/2, and those with more than 1.5% loss were harmed by the upgrade.

loc.heading: The connections that HTTP/2 left behind

facts.summary: 75% of Fastly edge connections were then in the loss range HTTP/2 improved; the rest split roughly evenly between hurt and unchanged, so 6 times as many transactions improved as were harmed.
facts.quote: 75% of Fastly edge connections at that time fell into the “improved by HTTP/2” range of packet loss and the remainders were split roughly evenly between hurt and unchanged. This was definitely a net win with 6 times as many HTTP transactions improved as harmed by the transition

loc.heading: The connections that HTTP/2 left behind

facts.summary: As of April 2020 the post says a thorough HTTP/3 performance analysis must wait for robust implementations deployed in diverse environments.
facts.quote: A thorough analysis of HTTP/3 performance will need to wait for a variety of robust implementations to be deployed in diverse environments.

facts.summary: HTTP/3's stated goal is that a loss-repair delay affects only one HTTP transaction while all transactions still share one aggregate sending rate; TCP orders all streams, QUIC orders each stream separately.
facts.quote: the scope of a single packet loss-driven repair delay should only apply to a single HTTP transaction. It needs to do so in a way that all the transactions coordinate their aggregate transmission rate. … TCP enforces the “in-order delivery” property on all the streams within the TCP session, while QUIC only enforces it within one stream at a time.

facts.summary: The post's illustration compares an HTTP/2 and an HTTP/3 connection, each with 5 mostly parallel transactions and a single early loss on the second transaction.
facts.quote: In each case the connection is made up of 5 mostly parallel HTTP transactions. Longer arrows indicate slower delivery times. Shortly after starting, each connection suffers a single packet loss to the second HTTP transaction in the connection.

facts.summary: HTTP/3 may not noticeably change performance for the average connection, especially when the HTTP/2 session has almost no loss and already follows TLS and TCP best practice.
facts.quote: HTTP/3 might not significantly affect performance for the average connection — or even affect it at all. This is especially true if the comparison HTTP/2 session has almost no packet loss and is already using best practice recommendations for TLS and TCP configurations.

loc.heading: The tail matters independent of the median

facts.summary: H2O schedules HTTP/2 responses with an O(1) scheduler that picks which response to send for every 16KB chunk.
facts.quote: The server implements a O(1) scheduler that determines which HTTP response should be sent to the client, per every 16KB chunk.

facts.summary: To switch quickly to a high-priority response, H2O says the TCP send buffer should hold only in-flight packets and TLS records must be small enough to avoid HOL blocking; the cost is more CPU and slightly higher latency.
facts.quote: In order to do so, send buffer of the TCP/IP stack should be kept empty except for the packets in-flight, and size of the TLS records must be small enough to avoid head-of-line blocking. The downside is that obeying the requirement increases the interaction between the server process and kernel, which result in consumption of more CPU cycles and slightly increased latency.

facts.summary: Since version 2.1, for connections with RTT above and CWND below the thresholds, H2O keeps unsent HTTP/2 frames minimal; its benchmarks suggest an average reduction of 1 RTT.
facts.quote: Starting from version 2.1, H2O provides directives that lets the users tune how the TCP/IP stack is used depending on the observed RTT, CWND, and the additional latency imposed by the interaction between the server and the OS. … For TCP/IP connections with greater RTT and smaller CWND than the configured threshold, the server will try to keep the size of HTTP/2 frames unsent as small as possible so that it can switch to sending a higher-priority response. Benchmarks suggest that users can expect in average 1 RTT reduction when this optimization is enabled.

facts.summary: The default thresholds are meant to activate the optimization on mobile and long-distance networks but not when a proxy sits on the path.
facts.quote: The default values of the thresholds have been chosen that the optimization will come into action for mobile and long-distance networks but not when a proxy exists on the network.

facts.summary: The optimization works only on Linux and OS X, which expose TCP_INFO and TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT.
facts.quote: The optimization is supported only on Linux and OS X. The two are the operating systems that provide access to TCP_INFO and an interface to adjust the size of the unsent buffer (TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT).

facts.summary: http2-latency-optimization-min-rtt is in milliseconds and defaults to 50; connections with a smaller RTT do not get the optimization, and 4294967295 disables it.
facts.quote: Latency optimization is disabled for TCP connections with smaller RTT (round-trip time) than the specified value. … Setting this value to 4294967295 (i.e. UINT_MAX) effectively disables the optimization. … http2-latency-optimization-min-rtt: 50

facts.summary: http2-latency-optimization-max-additional-delay, a ratio to RTT, defaults to 0.1; the optimization is off when the estimated extra delay from OS interaction exceeds it.
facts.quote: Maximum additional delay (as the ratio to RTT) permitted to get latency optimization activated. … http2-latency-optimization-max-additional-delay: 0.1

facts.summary: http2-latency-optimization-max-cwnd defaults to 65535 octets; above it the optimization stops and unsent HTTP/2 frames average slightly above the tcp_notsent_lowat sysctl value.
facts.quote: The server will not use or stop using latency optimization mode if CWND becomes greater than the configured value. In such case, average size of HTTP/2 frames buffered unsent will be slightly above the tcp_notsent_lowat sysctl value. … http2-latency-optimization-max-cwnd: 65535

facts.summary: http2-reprioritize-blocking-assets (default ON) sends highest-priority content types first only when the client does not use dependency-based prioritization.
facts.quote: if the client uses dependency-based prioritization, do not reprioritize … if the client does not use dependency-based prioritization, send the contents of which their types are given highest priority before any other responses … http2-reprioritize-blocking-assets: ON

facts.summary: http2-input-window-size, the HTTP/2 receive window for request bodies, defaults to 16777216 bytes.
facts.quote: Default window size for HTTP request body. … The value is the maximum amount of request body (in bytes) that can be sent by the client in 1 RTT (round-trip time). … 16777216

facts.summary: quiche 0.22.0's QPACK encoder writes Required Insert Count 0 and Base 0 in every field section prefix.
facts.quote: // Required Insert Count. encode_int(0, 0, 8, &mut b)?; … // Base. encode_int(0, 0, 7, &mut b)?;

facts.summary: Each field line is encoded only as a static-table index, a literal with a static name reference, or a fully literal line; the encoder has no dynamic-table path.
facts.quote: // Encode as statically indexed. … // Encode value as literal with static name reference. … // Encode as fully literal.

facts.summary: The quiche QPACK encoder struct has no fields, so it keeps no dynamic-table state.
facts.quote: /// A QPACK encoder. … #[derive(Default)] pub struct Encoder {}

conflicts.topic: how common loss above about 1.5 to 2% is
conflicts.note: S1 says even the worst cellular networks rarely exceed 2% loss; S2's 2016 edge data puts roughly half of the 25% non-improved connections in the 'hurt' band (above 1.5% loss). Thresholds, populations and years differ.
